[h1]Decide the fate of citizens of the world in this surveillance thriller![/h1]

You start the game by creating your character. Only gripe I have here is that there aren’t many choices as far as looks goes. It’d be nice to have more than one face type for the male and female. After that, you go through a very detailed tutorial that goes through the basics of what it will take to get you through the job you’ll be tasked with.

The game is deals with a story that’s shaped by your choices as you completed various assignments, gather evidence, flex your powers, and gather profiles. You don’t have to snoop either. As you progress through the game, you’ll have various choices that will allow you to take a stand against the very government organization you work for. A regular in-game cyber revolutionary. 

However, doing more for your boss means a higher clearance level and a higher clearance level means unlocking cooler (albeit creepier) powers, once classified information, lots more money and of course, prestige. With a higher salary, you can impress or intimidate your peers with purchases like new homes and more.

The game play is slow, but goes as fast as you want it to. I mean that in the sense that if you’re the type like me that combs through evidence and meticulously pieces together a person's profile, this will be the game for you. The main story clues are littered throughout your missions. So keep your eyes peeled. 

The music fits the narrative and the UI is clean. The developers are constantly listening and are active on the Steam Discussions. So, if there is a bug you come across, post to the Discussions and you can be sure a developer will take your problem into account. The only bug I came across was the weird save bug where my game would not save, but after a few updates, the saves are working.

I backed the game, but it's $14.99 and runs about 8-10 if you’re not rushing through it. You can definitely stretch that time out by investigating and going through the side content of which there’s a good amount of. The developers have said they plan on adding more content after the game’s ending and that you will be able to continue after your end of game save.

I recommend Need to Know: The Mass Surveillance Thriller Game. If you enjoy intrigue, espionage, and tools at your fingertips for finding out people’s secrets, then this game is for you. It’s a slow burn that works your detective skills and you can be either for or against the government. The game still has a few bugs, but the developers are quickly churning out updates and changelogs that address concerns.

review_text_raw:
In a nutshell: A good game, with some great ideas, that needs some polish on the execution, with a number of technical and interface issues that drag down a good story and a great idea.

Put simply, the idea of a game where you move through the hierarchy of a sinister spying agency is a great one, and this game's greatest success so far in my time with it has been not only showing how quickly the power to snoop on everything and everyone can go wrong, but also, and crucially, how it can still also be a force for good. The story is I think the strongest point of the game for me, because it's depiction of the ironically named 'Department of Liberty' is not really as some cartoon villain 'Illuminati conspiracy' but as a government organisation set up in response to a great crisis which, at least initially, is comprised largely of ordinary people. Sure, some of the people you meet in the game are dubiously motivated at best, but the game reinforces in the narrative consistently that there are good people in the DoL, who genuinely believe the spying they engage in is justified and indeed, there are examples in game where the power you use does make a real difference.

I can't say much more without spoiling the hell out of the game, but suffice it to say, if story is what you want, the game offers an intriguing story, and while it may not be a Tom Clancy tale, I've found it engaging and compelling.

Likewise, the gameplay offers good challenge, requiring you to carefully dissect the data you sift through, looking not just for keywords early on but as time goes on, looking for more complicated and easily missed details, like tracing suspicious bank activity with logs of suspicious contacts, and working out if they match up or are a red herring. These shifting challenges do a reasonably good job of building on each other, with each clearance level you go through iterating on previous challenges with an extra layer of complexity, and this organic growth of difficulty is largely well-executed. But it does lead into the big problem in the game: communication.

This game has a real problem communicating with the player, and I think it's largely down to an interface that can be clunky and unintuitive. Partially this is down to bugs, like notifications on your phone not displaying so you're left staring blankly waiting for something to happen, to more egregious errors like typos in the keywords you're looking for, and contextual menus being hard to close once opened and obscuring the screen. These are all fixable issues thankfully, and while irritating, they don't for me drag the game down too much, but the sooner they are resolved, the better, and they are likely to irritate some players too much to continue.

Also, the game can be ambiguous in what the objectives of each day actually require. For instance, you might be asked to look for keywords, but the game isn't good at indicating whether you need a literal, case-sensitive match of the word, or a contextual match. For instance, if the keyword was 'Bomb Kit' and you saw a log that said 'making my own bombs in a kit', you might well flag that as suspicious, and logically, it totally is, but because the game is looking for a case-sensitive, exact match, it marks you down as wrong for it. Again, these issues are not exactly common, but they're infrequent enough to annoy, and for me are the biggest issue of all in the game, but again, can be fixed by the devs.

So in the end, I recommend this game, but I do it with an advisory: if you want a good story, with fun challenges and an engaging concept of government intelligence and the morality of that, then I highly recommend it, but make sure you go in right now knowing there are currently technical and design issues, and while these will likely be fixed, as of the time of this review they exist, and they can annoy. Hopefully you'll be like me, and able to see through the roughness to the diamond within, and enjoy the experience for what it is, not what you necessarily would like it to be.

review_text_raw:
Very fun game that does an excellent job of portraying the slippery slope when dealing with the question of rights vs security.

*** Spoilers ***
You start off with basic tasks like hunting down murderers or catching terrorists, but then a hurricane hits...

... And you're not permitted to go snooping through people's offline data, but you break the law anyway because if you can track them down, you can send FEMA their location and save some lives! So it's fine, right? Sure, some people lose a bit of privacy, but you're rescuing them from the hurricane!

And then as you rise through the ranks you get a bit more power and you start dealing with tracking down serial killers or stopping an active shooter... But then a senator doesn't like the fact that your department is ignoring people's rights to privacy and wants to shut you down...

... So you blackmail her by digging through her data and finding embarassing information to damage her career. Can't have her foolish ideals stand in the way, obstructing your quest to save lives, right?

And then a bunch of corporations give you access to their data, making your job to track down terrorists even easier, and helping you along the way in your original mission to find a man who caused a few nuclear reactors to overload in a massive terrorist attack, but they want a couple favours...

... So you start doing a bit of corporate espionage on the side, but it's fine, I'm sure, because the backroom deals are how you make progress, and no one *really* needs to keep their shopping history private, do they?

But then some of this stuff gets leaked and more politicians start rallying against it. Fools. They don't know how hard you're working to keep this country safe! They don't know how necessary it is to use this data...

... So you launch a disinformation campaign to silence them and ruin their credibility. It was their fault anyways. They threatened the department, and you needed to protect it! You're the only one standing in the way of the terrorists attacking america, so getting your hands dirty sometimes is fine if it's to protect the greater good, right?

So throughout the game you're doing these underhanded deals, blackmail and character assassinations, but it's fine because you're catching terrorists, saving lives, and generally making sure the citizens can go on with their happy little lives. Soon it pays off! You catch a terrorist who leads you to a terrorist who leads you to a whole network of them! ... but they're scattered across the globe, and many of the countries aren't too keen on sending them to the states for judgement...

... Well they stand in your way! They're harbouring enemies of the state, that's basically an act of war, right? You need to show these governments the errors of their ways... Or maybe you can't. Maybe you should arm some of the militant groups in the countries who are more friendly towards US interests... So you start distributing arms to them and help them seize power, but it's fine, right? You toppled a government and installed a few dictatorships, but you've got to help your country! They were basically asking for it anyways by hiding your enemies, right? So what if a few thousand people on the otherside of the world got killed, you're supposed to protect Americans and that's what you're going to do!

But now your powers are growing and word of your department's actions are reaching the journalists, who are writing scathing criticisms of you and turning the people against you... Well you can't have that happen, so you need to silence them, either by getting them fired or threatening them to keep quiet! Freedom of speech is just getting in the way here, this sacrifice is for the good of the nation, right? Right?!

Despite your best efforts public opinion is still slowly turning against you, and the politicians are noticing... well there's an election coming up, so you've got to make sure a politician friendly to your department gets in. Can't have the president disband the department of liberty, there's still so much work left to do! 

... So you blackmail politicians, leak incriminating documents, and funnel support towards your prefered candidate, ensuring she wins the election. You've subverted democracy but it's fine, right? You need to protect the department because it protects the nation! You're the hero of this story after all! You can't let people who don't understand get in the way, right guys? Right?! Sacrifices must be made! It's for the good of the nation! The good of us all! There's no way I could be the villain, right?! I am the hero here!!!!

But of course, it doesn't stop there. You need more power. Even when you're launching military assaults on embassies in foreign nations, even when you drone-strike your own citizens, even when you assassinate the leaders of other countries who once tried to help you but now stand in your way... 

And then you see it. You get betrayed. People want the power your department has, and your boss and other corporations are vying for the systems that now control the world. What was a perfect, all-seeing system is being used as a pawn by people for petty power plays and revenge... to further their own ideals at the expense of everyone else. You know that you need to end this. You need to stop it. The people at the top need to be brought down. A system this powerful can't remain in the hands of those who would abuse it. A system this perfect either needs to be destroyed or to remain under the control of someone who would use it for good... someone like you... And after all, you're the hero, so why not take it? It's for the good of the nation after all... 

*** End Spoilers ***

Unfortunately there's still a few problems with the game. The interface is not nearly as responsive as it should be for as simple a game as this is. Additionally when you get assignments cross-referencing between multiple suspects,... ugh... the limitations of the UI really make themselves known, and despite there being hundreds of HCI papers out there for how to build proper interfaces when comparing data, this game chooses to use none of them. As someone who worked in an Info-vis lab for a while, I can safely say that the method they chose to link data between two different suspects is one of the most annoying and tedious ways they could have possibly done it. You will audiably groan when you see the mission rules "Link evidence when two suspects travel to the same city at the same time.". It is that bad. Fortunately these missions are few and far between, so you don't have to deal with it too often.

I also didn't like that your actions basically had no lasting effects. Any big choice either ends the game or lets you continue playing. I was really hoping that...

*** Spoilers ***
When you get betrayed, you would have a chance to work with the Snow Owl black-ops division instead of with Tripwire to work your way back up to the top. Maybe based on which faction you had a higher reputation with. They're black-ops anyways, with everything they do being classified and deniable, so helping you wouldn't be completely out of the question.
*** End Spoilers ***

That aside, the game was very fun and very satisfying to play. It played around with a lot of neat ideas, and again, I really liked the story. I also liked how it showed your progression from living in a trashy apartment and working in basically a basement closet to living in a super upscale neighbourhood and leading your own division as you progress through the ranks. I highly recommend it.

8/10

I was really looking forward to this game but thus far I have to say it has been a disappointment.
I have only just started playing it but am already overwhelmed with the bugs and poor interface design issues. 
It gives you simple tasks yet the means to interact with the displays is plagued with problems both in its design and what appear to be bugs.

Just listing out the issues I ran into I can think of:
- Depending on your resolution important parts of the screen will be cut off and unreadable
- Phone rang after my first day and I was simply unable to click the answer button.
- Rules window becomes stuck in the up position covering up all other windows. Had to restart the mission to clear that up.
- Trying to change your tool to another tool causes windows to close that you wanted to use the tool to click on
- Rules window is very often covered up by the window of evidence you are trying to flag making it impossible to read the rules to choose the right one
- Clipboard window often does the same thing covering up things that you wanted to click on.
- No indication on the screen to guide you as to how to actually start your mission. Button to start work is the same button to view your overall status. Extremely confusing and no good feedback as to the current state.
- Clicking on the pyramid helper opens up a series of help tips but the window doesnt pop up making it impossible to scroll or view
- Rules window, when minimized, allows you to scroll but its such a small sliver its pointless. Why not just make this thing either minimized or full sized, why let it function at all in its minimized form other than to click on it and maximize it?

Overall the concept is interesting and I am still hopeful for imporovements. But thus far I am going to wait longer to give it another go.

[quote]Edit Saturday, November 3, 2018:
As a Monomyth developer posted below this review, this game has changed a lot since it's release and since I wrote this review. While I do not currently have time to give the game another shot due to classes, keep in mind that the review below is not an accurate reflection of the current version of Need to Know.
[/quote]

So I tried to like this game, I really did, and I was one of the ones who followed the hype from the first trailer release in the Kickstarter campaign. I really looked forward to the Papers, Please -eqsue surveillance game that the trailers advertised. Holding out to release (remember, no pre-orders!), however, revealed some key flaws that the game has.

[h1]Lack of Tutorial[/h1]
The lack of a tutorial is my primary issue with Need to Know. With almost zero instruction given, the player has no clue on how to progress, how to use the different tools provided in-game, and what distinguishes a subject between a "safe" individual and a threat. Players are expected to know beforehand what all the tools do and how to use them effectively, and  with the game not arming the players with that knowledge, I and many others were left confused as to what to do almost constantly.

[h1]User Interface[/h1]
The current user interface is extremely similar to the user interface that was advertised throughout the developer cycle. While it seems to be extremely sleek and inviting, don't let its looks fool you. The UI was another primary issue with Need to Know. In practice, the UI was sluggish and huge on-screen, with every single element in each window being blown up unnecessarily. Everything except any back or close indicators, which took minutes to find on several occasions. In the beginning of the game, it even took me about 10 minutes to figure out how to begin the first mission! 

[h1]Final Evidence is not consistent with Evidence Requirements[/h1]
At the beginning of each mission, you are given specific key evidence to look out for while analyzing individuals. Several times, the evidence the game wanted me to find were inconsistent with the requirements it gave me. This meant I often “missed” evidence which was never actually listed as a requirement.

[h1]Inconsistent Results after Missions[/h1]
As part of the story, you need to build up your agency's trust in you by successfully analyzing, identifying key elements a suspect might exhibit, and eventually classifying the subject as safe or a threat. These trust points given, however, were often inconsistent. Successfully classify and identify all pieces of evidence in a mission? Have 15 trust points! Missed one piece of evidence? There goes 30 points!

[h1]Inconsistent Dialogue[/h1]
Have a bad day and lose a lot of trust points? Doesn't matter, your boss will let you know what a great job you did today!

[h1]Bugs and Glitches[/h1]
While many people (such as myself) disregard the bug warnings in games and play them anyway only to still have a positive experience, let me tell you that it is not the case with this game. I've enjoyed this game when it's made sense, unfortunately as you progress it gets more and more convoluted and less and less consistent in the results it gives you.

Firstly, the lack of tutorials is a glaring omission, having to try and work out what you're supposed to do can be frustrating at times.

Secondly: The interface is unresponsive and a bit of a mess. Having to cover a chunk of your screen real estate with the 'requirements' panel makes it hard to look at evidence and requirements at the same time, and having to click on your badge to start the mission with no hint whatsoever is a massive oversight.

My major bugbear however: Sometimes you miss evidence because it wasn't actually in the requirements. Other times, you flag evidence that matches the requirements, but apparently one or two specific pieces don't count. The most infuriating example of this I found was when a name was misspelled - an O had been substituted for an A, which led me to believe that it wasn't a match for what I was looking for (often homonyms or similar spellings are used to try and throw you off). In this case, it was an actual spelling mistake that had somehow made it through to the final product. Errors like this are a dealbreaker for me - It adds too much of a random element to the game, especially when the penalties for missing something or getting something wrong are so severe.

About those penalties: Get everything right from a pool of 18 and you'll get a modest boost, miss a couple of things out of a pool of 20 and you lose a ton of points. Balance is totally off, and because it's a 100% scale, knocking it out of the park early on doesn't buffer you against getting screwed by inconistent missions later on.

Bugs-wise, the only ones I've seen so far are message alerts on your phone flashing up so quick that you'll miss them if you blink, and a conversation going on whilst I was supposed to be doing something else. Nothing game-breaking yet, but I wouldn't be surprised if I found something more problematic in future.

Until the inconsistencies are fixed, I can't recommend this game. It's frustrating, as it had so much potential and I really wanted to like it.

I like the premise and gameplay of this game, but so far - after 16 hours - the story advancement has been miniscule. And judging by the progress in "clearance levels" I'm in like half of the game. And it's pretty unrewarding and just really, really long. The core gameplay loop is pretty nice when you get different mission types or advancements in the story, but when you spread it over so many hours it becomes boring anyway.

I also believe there is an issue with difficulty, since there's no option to change it, and for the first like 4 or more clearance levels it is ridiculously easy (with one very hard mission thrown in every once in a while). But there's really no punishment for failure in story sense - you can absolutely botch an "investigation" (when you are for example looking for a suspect in waves and accidentally mark them as non-suspect in the first wave) and still succeed. Which makes sense from gameplay sense, but it's pretty immersion breaking, especially when you are still awarded with catching the criminal and such.

And coming from there - a lot of stuff in the game feels very forced. Like your "romance" / "date" or whatever just eventually appears in your apartment with no option to reject them. Sometimes you are presented with "options", but when you choose certain dialogues the game just ends (sometimes as if you almost won, and sometimes you just end up in jail and such) but in the end you always have to go back and choose the options the game wants you to.

And speaking of "going back" - there are no save slots; The game saves randomly and you can't go back. If you fuck something up because there was no tutorial or the description was misleading or you didn't get the gist of what you are looking for - tough luck, the game punishes you for that and you have to keep going forward. This issue is especially apparent with some mission types or evidence gathering that's poorly explained. One time I got everything wrong for misreading what the game wanted me to do (matching years of consecutive growth when something happens vs. matching just the last year of consecutive growth *with the thing that happened*). And there is more where that comes from.

I also encountered some minor visual bugs and UI annoyances. One of the bigger one is that "helpers" (people who you don't use your powers on and only help match evidence and such) are marked the same color on the map as the suspects. Well, some times. From the tutorial I think they are meant to be teal, but they're white like everyone else... Unless they are red for some reason, but only every once in a while (even in a single mission) before they are white again.

All in all I'm pretty conflicted in whether to recommend this game - [b]if you really like the core gameplay loop (go watch some videos) then sure, go for it[/b]. The annoyances are minor enough to really affect that too much. But [b]if you are like me, spending 16 hours to get into what is presumably half of the game with very repetitive gameplay and just tiny bits of story... You are better spending your time elsewhere[/b]. Just for comparison: I finished the whole playthrough of Prey 2017 in like 22 hours, and by the time I was at hour 16 I had discovered almost all of the story, everything about the station and Typhon, etc.

review_text_raw:
Very much enjoying this game so far! Great scripting, interesting storyline, unique cartoonish style that matches the theme of the game! I have become quite engrossed with the characters and their interactions. There has been a lot of thought gone into making these characters seem realistic and this game has already touched on some unsettling aspects related to mass surveilance within the first hour of gameplay.

The game has been easy to play and I didn't fail the interview (think of Men in Black alien test)! Not sure if this is because the devs fixed the tutorial thing, but I have had no problems so far - it has all seemed pretty straight-forward to me! 

The missions have been quite fun. I'm still at clearance level 10, but I can see how this will get harder. So far I have encountered one bug, but I signed out then in again and it was fine. Obviously as more updates come through this will be less frequent, but once I was into the third mission I had already forgotten!

I think the UI is supposed to represent a work-desk and I quite like the style. I'm playing on a big screen and I know where I need to focus becuase it's pretty clear when the phone is to be used, and when other various controls are to be used. If I'm in doubt, all I've needed to do is click or hover and discover different aspects to the controls. I appreciated the artistic license used in screen composition when the dialogue is going on.

So far I have gotten a little bit impatient with Peepr, i.e. when I had to sign back in, but you can click and the dialogue goes faster. Added functionality with the skip option would be nice but so far this has been minor for me.

I did not follow the kickstarter campaign but a friend recommended it to me because I often like a game with a story to tell - and Need To Know hasn't disappointed me thus far! I'll update this review as I play more.

EDIT: I changed from not recommended to recommended. Because the game (tactics) change after reaching clearance level 8. Still the below criticizm is applied, but for a game with this pricetag it doesn't to that bad.

So i was hyped for this game from the start & a early kickstarter funder, but it feels like a disappointment for now.
I specially played this game for a few hours to see if it just has a slow start. But sadly it doesn't only have a slow start.. It keeps slow (might even call it boring). 
Only positive note i have at this moment is, that the story is well written and has some noticable real life scenarios.

Another bad thing (in my opinion) is the time it takes to unlock new ablilities. This only happens when you reach a new/higer clearence level. 
I have more then 4 hours into the game. And i only just unlocked clearance level 8 and therby new abilities. This takes to long in my opinion..

The game has the "beta" feel all over itself. Feels cluncky, UI is horrible to work with & windows get blocked constantly. Rules window should be movable at least.
Crashes at weird moments and nothings happening at the same point after restarting the game.

Also the evidence that needs to be collected, can be very conflicting. The rules states that something needs to be collected. But it it isn't directly linked to your suspect but a contact. The game states that you made a wrong choice.

Just as many i was hoping for a "Papers, Please" like gameplay and challenge, but than in a intelligence styled jacket.
This game is disappointing on all fonts:
- Gets boring soon, game also needs some kind of speed mode.
- Sometimes very unclear/conflicting what kind of evidence needs to be collected.
- You get new ways to check on people but no new tools to use, but only whit new clearance levels.
- Just point and click/memory playstyle. I miss some sort of typing involved (for example keyboard shortcuts), playing as an analist.
- Some times theres logic in "linking" people or suspects together early on. You just/simply can't... This is only possible when the game tells you to.
- (to hide spoilers) You do the same thing anywere.
- Buying stuff.. Ehh, whats the use of this? Whats the use of making money in this game anyway. I don't even have to pay rent.. 
- Weird saving structure. Log out before "End Session" aaaand start all over again with the same mission.
- When you "start over" a session by quitting the game. The location and names of the suspects is the same every time & also their logs.
- Crashes mid game (had three in less than 4 hours of gameplay).

It's just constantly doing the same thing.. Over and over.
This is the thing with most games and isn't that big of an issue. 

The issue with this game is, that there isn't enough variation in "what" to do. 
There is just to little to do to keep it interesting. It's way too late in the game & taking way too long to get there, if you even get there you're interest in this game is most likely already gone.

Still putting all the negative points aside. For their first (major) game, it's actually quite good.
I'm certain they will improve the game and crush some bugs in the oncoming days. So lets see how this plays out!

I'll put a summary at the bottom where it's segmented off from the spoiler area.

Game's great. Would recommend.


---------SPOILER TERRITORY. SORRY I COULDN'T FIGURE OUT THE FORMATTING---------


The story is fairly well written. It can be a little iffy at times when it comes to the grand scheme of things, but if you hold your suspension of disbelief, mainly the idea that someone could rise through the ranks like that and that you are pretty much the lynchpin for everything that happens in the story, it works well. I do wish that there were more outs from the story as time goes by, but you can only put so many options into a game before you start over-writing it. 
While I'm talking about endings, I'll bring up probably my least favorite one. One of the final endings is just one or two sentences and then it boots you back to the main menu. I get that they weren't trying to take a side in the underlying debate in the game, but it does seem a little strange when you have dialogue choices mean almost the exact same thing multiple times in the story.
I love how the characters are implemented into the story. On Day 2 meet someone who has your back. And that same person is with you until the final major decision. He's well developed and seems almost human with the way he's written, having real motivations behind his actions that are very relatable to many people. Almost every main character you interact with has an effect on the story if they don't straight up give you a way out of the story. For those that don't give you a way out, they still plant seeds into your mind. What those seeds may be will vary and what they grow into is up to you, but the fact still remains that they have really thought the writing out.
The mechanics of the game have also been very thought out. It may look like dots on a map when you first start out, but it quickly expands when you hover over that dot. A name and a picture along with a general location does enough to put meaning into a character that will be on your screen for about a minute. And then there's more information on the person once you click on them, information that will almost never have an impact on the case at hand. As you go through their data, it plants more seeds of doubt in the system. And then you have to click one of two buttons. Do they go free, or do they not go free? No matter what button you click, there will be text that pops up. That text tells you what happens to that person. Solely because of what you decided to do. The weight behind all that is monumental at times. It makes you question your decisions at times. And it is absolutely well done.
The commentary on the security/liberty debate is where this game really shines. By establishing a connection with someone who will be on your side until the end of the game, it ensures that the line for most people will be blurred. It's story is written well enough to have it come out to you at points and ask you if what you are doing is right and warns you that it's a dangerous path that lies ahead if you continue down it. As you keep climbing the ladder at the DoL, it's not just the people around you that starts to make you question the morality of everything that happens here. That's before you start to notice that the decisions are starting to become less and less mundane as time goes by. And as it all comes to a head, there's one question in your mind:
How much are you willing to sacrifice for security?
This question meshes in well with other subplots in the story, whether it be surviving though nepotism or just trying to live a normal life. You see people early in the game have moral dilemmas when they have to do things like authorize a new technology early or have to decide on where to take their career. Adds a nice bit of background to the characters you meet along the way.


---------[END SPOILER TERRITORY]---------


All in all, this is a fantastic game. It's entertaining, has a well-written story, and has a lot of deep questions that you have to ask yourself as technology advances in today's world. Takes a bit of time to complete. It took me about 16 hours to do my first full run of it. And it was 16 hours well spent.

Final Ratings:
Story: 8/10
Need a little bit of suspension of disbelief to get the ball rolling, but once the ball does get rolling it's hard to stop it. Excellent twist that you can just straight up miss if you're not paying attention.
UI: 6/10
Hope you like dots. You'll be seeing them almost exclusively. Does contribute well to the whole computerized atmosphere of the game. Sometimes Person(s) Of Interest (POI) get lost in the southern side of the map or in places that aren't really in conventional areas (looking at you Alaska and Hawaii). Sometimes the UI overlaps itself if you click a button too early and there's dialogue or if there's a POI on the eastern side of the map in the space between the phone and what the office around you looks like. Map scrolling can be annoying, so you disable it and then it's annoying that it isn't scrolling, so you re-enable it and the scrolling gets annoying again, and then you get annoyed that you have to toggle this on and off so you just leave it one or the other an deal with it.
Music: 7/10
Can get a little repetitive with some of the longer levels, but it's pretty well written. It's electronic style fits well with the setting of the game. Musical cues also help out in some scenarios.
Commentary: 10/10
Can't go into too much detail without spoiling a lot of the game. If you don't care about spoilers, go back up and reread the section that I start by mentioning the commentary.
Overall: 8/10
It's fun.

He's well developed and seems almost human with the way he's written, having real motivations behind his actions that are very relatable to many people. Almost every main character you interact with has an effect on the story if they don't straight up give you a way out of the story. For those that don't give you a way out, they still plant seeds into your mind. What those seeds may be will vary and what they grow into is up to you, but the fact still remains that they have really thought the writing out. The mechanics of the game have also been very thought out. It may look like dots on a map when you first start out, but it quickly expands when you hover over that dot. A name and a picture along with a general location does enough to put meaning into a character that will be on your screen for about a minute. And then there's more information on the person once you click on them, information that will almost never have an impact on the case at hand. As you go through their data, it plants more seeds of doubt in the system. And then you have to click one of two buttons. Do they go free, or do they not go free? No matter what button you click, there will be text that pops up. That text tells you what happens to that person. Solely because of what you decided to do. The weight behind all that is monumental at times. It makes you question your decisions at times. And it is absolutely well done. The commentary on the security/liberty debate is where this game really shines. By establishing a connection with someone who will be on your side until the end of the game, it ensures that the line for most people will be blurred. It's story is written well enough to have it come out to you at points and ask you if what you are doing is right and warns you that it's a dangerous path that lies ahead if you continue down it. As you keep climbing the ladder at the DoL, it's not just the people around you that starts to make you question the morality of everything that happens here. That's before you start to notice that the decisions are starting to become less and less mundane as time goes by. And as it all comes to a head, there's one question in your mind: How much are you willing to sacrifice for security? This question meshes in well with other subplots in the story, whether it be surviving though nepotism or just trying to live a normal life. You see people early in the game have moral dilemmas when they have to do things like authorize a new technology early or have to decide on where to take their career. Adds a nice bit of background to the characters you meet along the way. ---------[END SPOILER TERRITORY]--------- All in all, this is a fantastic game. It's entertaining, has a well-written story, and has a lot of deep questions that you have to ask yourself as technology advances in today's world. Takes a bit of time to complete. It took me about 16 hours to do my first full run of it. And it was 16 hours well spent. Final Ratings: Story: 8/10 Need a little bit of suspension of disbelief to get the ball rolling, but once the ball does get rolling it's hard to stop it. Excellent twist that you can just straight up miss if you're not paying attention. UI: 6/10 Hope you like dots. You'll be seeing them almost exclusively. Does contribute well to the whole computerized atmosphere of the game. Sometimes Person(s) Of Interest (POI) get lost in the southern side of the map or in places that aren't really in conventional areas (looking at you Alaska and Hawaii). Sometimes the UI overlaps itself if you click a button too early and there's dialogue or if there's a POI on the eastern side of the map in the space between the phone and what the office around you looks like. Map scrolling can be annoying, so you disable it and then it's annoying that it isn't scrolling, so you re-enable it and the scrolling gets annoying again, and then you get annoyed that you have to toggle this on and off so you just leave it one or the other an deal with it. Music: 7/10 Can get a little repetitive with some of the longer levels, but it's pretty well written. It's electronic style fits well with the setting of the game. Musical cues also help out in some scenarios. Commentary: 10/10 Can't go into too much detail without spoiling a lot of the game. If you don't care about spoilers, go back up and reread the section that I start by mentioning the commentary. Overall: 8/10 It's fun.

Ok, so I've been waiting for this game for so long. First, I was extremely hyped up. After playing demo for some time my enthusiasm went down a bit, mainly because of lack of real, engaging gameplay, very clunky interface and lack of clarity in every screen in the game. Still, game looked beautiful with it's cartoon style and many cool symbols, graphics, and so. And now finally it's out. While I still think that this kind of a game has great potential (UPLINK, anyone?), unfortunately Need to Know is very hard to enjoy, despite it's visual charm. 

First, there are so many small, but annoying things, like unresponsivness or lack of skip button during certain screens. There's a lot of it in this game, and I wonder why those things weren't eliminated during long developement time. 

Second, despite the fact that the game looks great, the whole interface is a confusing mess. It is so hard to figure out what you are supposed to do, there are so many buttons and aditional cards around and no tutorial. It is so confusing, since so much is just randomly generated and serves just as an extra, cause...

Third. The gameplay. It is actually a memory clicking game (Think of it as a very flawed "Papers Please"). Granted, I played for an hour or two, but it gets repetitive already, and it doesn't feel real at all. There is no real suspense, just randomly generated trivia facts and phrases you have to find as fast as you can. It's no fun, at least for me. No excitement, no immersion. 

I'm sure the game gets more complex after a while: there is shop app in your phone and some stuff to buy, there are new "powers" that you unlock while advancing in the ranks of the agency, but everything feels undeveloped, almost like a free mobile game. And that's a shame, cause the visual style is (again) amazing, and the story is at least ok. So, maybe in Need To Know 2? 

Pros:
- Cool visual style
- Exciting topic 
- Modernately interesting story 

Cons:
- TERRIBLE interface
- Repetitive and almost non-existent gameplay
- Really annoying mechanics choices (No skip button? C'mon...)

Eventually, it's a no, unless you are willing to play repetitive memo / visual novel game and are patient enough to constantly fight with the interface.

I really wanted to like this game.  I love the premise, I love the feeling of detective work and secret-selling, and the narrative for me was more interesting and less stressful than Papers Please, which is easily the game it most resembles.

Unfortunately, the game is buggy, and on top of that, the process of identifying evidence or tying pieces together is so painfully unintuitive that it kills the enjoyment.  On top of that, the pace is absolutely glacial.  Assuming the idea is that you are working your way up from a rookie at the alternate universe NSA to ultimate shadow broker, I expected to be quite a bit further than 3 levels in at the six hour mark.   How much of that time was eaten up by really pointless missions that don't seem to tie into the narrative or plot?   Quite a bit.

And then there's the penalty for failure.  Woe unto the one that misunderstands the instructions for how to handle your pieces of evidence.   If you don't figure it out, you can lose a metric crap-ton of "compliance", which is the game's meter for how well you're doing.   I went from 97% compliance to 33% in a single mission.  It doesn't really give you much partial credit - if you recognize something is off about a person, but you don't mark it exactly correctly, it's nearly as bad as missing the clue entirely.   

I think that's what's really broken about this game at the end.  The part where you know in your gut when someone is clearly a problem or dangerous, but the game doesn't seem to recognize your efforts and punishes you for trying.   Having worked in government, I can say that's accurate in terms of simulating the job experience, but it's not fun.   Not at all.

review_text_raw:
Good game for mature children and teens, but most adults will be disappointed. The main game mechanic is "finding a needle in a haystack". Unfortunately, the haystack is tiny, and the needles are not very well hidden. You are provided a list of keywords to find in tiny documents, given basic criteria. The biggest challenge is making sure it is spelled correctly before highlighting it. I expected the game to be more investigatory, being able to follow leads, etc... this is not that kind of game.

Your character is a young adult, fresh out of college, working his/her first job. The story and the style of the dialogue was written to appeal to children. At one point, my friend in the game texts me to ask who was my high school crush. I immediately assume he is phishing for the answer to my security question to hack my password, but no. I'm overthinking. The game just does this to determine if your crush was a male or female, so it can introduce a new character into the game.

The icing on the cake for why I have to give this game a thumbs down... An anti-government group tries to extort me. There is no option to report this to the Department. I choose not to provide them any documents, because I take national security seriously, and then I lose the game. ---You must leak classified documents, or it is game over.

So much for Monomyth Games' "will you stand up for privacy, or help create an unstoppable police state?" ---Well, I'm forced to leak classified documents to terrorists, so I guess I don't have much choice in the matter.

Monomyth Games also writes, "You can also resist ... by aiding underground groups ... Or, you can just use all of that juicy classified information for your own personal gain. Your call." ---But it's not my call, because if you don't leak the classified information, it is game over.

The pitch made about the game misrepresents the actual game. I would have paid twice as much for the game if it delivered on what was promised, but as it is, I feel duped. They did a really good job on the graphics and interface design... moral dilemmas in stories are awesome, but you can't propose a moral dilemma to the player and then force a game over state if they choose to follow federal law.

EDIT: After playing an additional 14 hours, I felt it was best to revise my original review. I can rate this game as being recommended, so long as you're okay with a few necessary compromises. I'll explain those below.

I wanted to like this game very badly, but 5 hours in and I'm starting to see the seams and cracks that make this a less than perfect experience. I think my dissatisfaction with the gameplay comes down to one question: when you played Papers, Please, was your favorite part of the game the times where you had to squint at the IDs to see if that was a D or a P or a G? If so, you'll love this game. Everyone else will be irritated, and rightfully so.

The game is beautiful - I loved the interface and the art style. The story, at least so far, is passable and engaging, and I'm conflicted about finishing the game because of its flaws and the main reason is because I do want to see how the story resolves itself, and there's an early "flash-forward" that has me intrigued about what remains to be experienced.

But when the core gameplay is "spot the difference between two letters or numbers" or "try to remember this ridiculously complex flow chart of rules and protocols", it gets exhausting. It also doesn't help that for me, the game was slow and plodding at times. Opening up a menu sometimes took 2 or 3 seconds longer than you expected it to, and visual transitions sometimes slowed to a crawl. Add to that the completely boring gameplay loops and you have a recipe for boredom.

So again, to summarize... if you have fun deciding which of these three names - P Vasquez and D Vasqez and B Vaskez - matches the one in a briefing supplied to you before the stage begins, and you can suspend your disbelief that so many people would have more than one variation of the same name in their address books, then you'll like the game. Otherwise, maybe read a plot summary.

UPDATE: I stuck with the game because of the story, as I mentioned. And I was surprised to see - well into the game - that the gameplay does get mixed up in interesting ways eventually. There are still lots of repetitive tasks that seem to be there just because, at the end of the day, this is a game and not a true simulation. But there was something to the premise and the characterization and dialogue that kept me wanting to press forward even when it was monotonous. If you think you're up for the task and have nearly 20 hours to spare, the ending is passable.

review_text_raw:
[b] Premise [/b]
You are a government employee working for the 'Department of Liberty' where your job is to spy on/profile suspects and targets. You 'match' pertinent information (dating profile, purchases, social media posts) to mission based criteria. 

[b] Play it if you like.... [/b]
If you played and enjoyed 'Papers, Please',  or 'Orwell' then chances are you'll like this game. If you like the concepts of 1984, V for Vendetta then you'll enjoy the story. And if you really just like sorting and matching information like a nerd (like me) then you'll love the gameplay

[b] Pros [/b]
Great gameplay concept and the profiling aspects are really interesting - a lot of thought has been put into these elements and I enjoyed seeing what I'd get access to next.
Progression through the 'ranks' is done at a decent pace which keeps things fresh. Theres also some evening missions to supplement your income
Theres also a nice mix of mission types - I enjoyed the 'waves' missions where you are given more information each 'wave' in order to keep or eliminate a suspect. 
Plenty of moral ambiguity to the main characters - although some are cartoonish. 
Overall story is quite compelling and I was always eager to see how it would progress (I did a lot of 'Oh I'll just play one more mission before I switch off.....')
Again, if you're an information-sorting nerd like me you'll just love the gameplay.

[b] Cons [/b]
UI is a bit painful sometimes - you can't zoom into information (you can change the UI to either 'IN YOUR FACE' or 'far away' but neither is a good compromise). For example when I had to look at a persons job on their social network it was so tiny I could barely make it out. And again when selecting suspects from a clustered area I couldn't highlight the right profile. I think this could be improved by making better use of the screen...there is SO MUCH empty space! I like to have the mission rules up all the time to match to but I constantly have to scroll through them at the bottom of the screen even though there was a huge empty space to the left of the screen totally un-used.
Story con - like a lot of these games you're given the illusion of freedom of choice. 

[b] Overall [/b]
I played the game through in 25 hours and was fully addicted to it as I was playing it. I think it just avoided getting stale mainly because the main story always kicked in at the right moments. If the UI could be sorted I'd have been so much happier.

As it stands the current version is pretty much just the beta with more content and more bugs. The game is riddled with tiny bugs and typos that would have been found by a normal group of testers. It's also riddled with usability issues.

[list]
[*] The lack of a clear tutorial is confusing - and piecing together how you're supposed to go about things using peepr is a PITA.
[*] The UI is stale and unintuitive. Very few of the buttons in the UI you need to press are actually animated - with no indication you've moused over them or that they are a button.
[*] Another UI issue - no skip buttons? No way to skip over cutscenes.
[*] Lack of customization - why even offer a screen to customize your character when you've got 3 combinations?
[/list]

Overall with those usability issues and the current bugs, I'm going to have to say I can't recommend this. Follow the project, see if they fix things up in a timely manner - but if you didn't already buy it years ago - you're probably better off waiting to see if you can get a better experience.

- On the other hand I was sitting on 100% compliance for a couple of days, and i didn't get any benefit from it. Initially i thought you move through the levels according to your performance, but unfortunately it's all scripted. I understand it would be difficult, still a nice change if the devs could implement this.

Still it's so irrelevant, probably you won't even remember what was in their profiles, and even if they appear ingame later, you won't remember that you've already seen them. Also I hate that the map is moving, it just gives an extra level of frustration, that i need to drag the map between profiles.
Sorry devs, I need to compare it to Papers, please. Need to know has a much wider scale, potential and story, still PP has much  more flavor, and there you can really feel the weight of your decisions.

The game description says: "You must spy on people’s deepest secrets, pick apart their private lives, and determine how dangerous they are. You can also resist these suffocating privacy invasions by aiding underground groups in leaking data to the media. Or, you can just use all of that juicy classified information for your own personal gain. Your call."

I took this statement literally, and after my first major 'choice', I was told I failed and the game returned to the menu screen.

Now don't get me wrong. I have no problem with fail conditions in games, or even perma-death consquences to actions, but this fail condition was so illogical that it is [i]exceptionally[/i] unique amongst my experiences with video games and choice-driven RPGs. It went like this:

[spoiler]Civilian privacy protection group (TripWire) asks me to sell classified data to them instead of to an internal operative within the department itself. When they ask, I refuse.

Nevermind what you tell them, the game adds them to your buyer list anyway and assigns them a relationship meter. 

When I don't sell data to them the very first time I have the opportunity, and the relationship meter reaches 0, I get this text at the game-over screen:

"TripWire became dissatisfied with your lack of assistance and notified the Department. You have been arrested for treason."

Arrested for treason....for [i]not[/i] selling classified government data to an outside group.[/spoiler]

Choice is expressly offered in the game description, but the choices are pointless when they merely determine [i]if[/i] you can continue instead of [i]how[/i] you continue.

Couple this with a lot of bugs, lack of tutorial and cluttered, clunky UI, and I simply can't recommend it in it's current state.

The game shows promise, but it needs polishing.

I really wanted to like this game. I saw Jon from MATN on Youtube try it and it looked liked my kind of thing. While I really like the premise, how it looks and some of the missions, unfortunately the experience has been frustrating. Mostly small things, but many small things which add up to an overall frustrating experience.

My general frustrations have been:
- Cluttered screen, especially when using a laptop when the screen is smaller.
- Evidence not demonstrating what the rules require but marked as missed when not chosen. (E.g. Evidence of someone telling a suspect to buy shares, when the rule says suspect must have bought shares. These are not the same thing, but the game considers them to be.)
- Moving background makes selecting the small dots difficult and no option to turn the movement off.
- You can choose incorrect evidence yet the immediate feedback says something which suggests it was in fact correct.
- Some rules weren't fully explained either in tutorial or in Peepr so got confused especially in the beginning.
- No way to re-evaluate a suspect once you've made a decision even if the day hasn't ended.
- No way to replay a day or restart unless you log out.
- Strongbox missions are sometimes very long winded and so get fed up quickly as the strongbox only seems to allow as much evidence as you can fit on the screen without scrolling. When on a 13inch macbook it fills up too quickly.

I think this game has a lot of promise, but it needs working on before I will consider recommending it.

I think I'm about halfway through with this game. It's very clear that Monomyth Games has put in a ton of time and effort into making this game really varied and fun. That being said, here are the major issues that I have with the game so far that make me closer to a "neutral" recommendation:

-UI is *very* clunky. Backing out of a profile or even trying to figure out how to end your very first day are both insanely unintuitive. This is fixable, and I have no doubt Monomyth is on it.

-Some weird prompts that have game-long consequences, but you have no idea at the time. For example, (mild spoiler) [spoiler] you get a text early on in the game asking if you used to like "Max" or "Serena" from high school. No indication at all that it's romantic, or that Max is a man. If you pick Max, you are now gay for the rest of the game. [/spoiler] Not anything major at all, but just... strange. 

-Doing "side by side" comparisons (i.e. "Try to find out the real profile, given these archived profiles of former criminals") are very hard to do, mainly because of the clunky UI. You can only have 1 profile at a time, and you can only save a certain amount of evidence to compare side-by-side at once. I wish you could have 2+ profiles open, especially since a lot of cases in the game require you to do side-by-side comparisons.

Regardless of these issues, if you're willing to have some patience for these developers, I still highly recommend the game. This game is basically "Papers, Please" but NSA-esque. You unlock more and more tools as you go along such as: [spoiler] social media posts, call metadata, audio recordings of calls, package tracking... you name it. [/spoiler]. As I said, it's very clear the company has put a ton of time into this game and want it to be fun.

This game is like Papers, Please where you examine documents according to daily rules,. However, this interface-heavy game fail in both UI & UX fronts. The UI elements is buggy and in the way almost every day. Animations are slow, and you wish it would go faster. I don't even know if there's a time limit because no UI explicitly tell you that (maybe they tell you that in the manual, but good UI doesn't need manual). The "Live" information display only show one line, and often hide information. UI elements obscure subjects in corners of the map (like Alaska, Australia). UX is bad because you cannot open multiple suspects at once, while some mission objective ask you to compare information across several suspects. Large part of the UI are unusable space.

There's some story that might be interesting, with eleemnts from real world. But it's full of filler missions that make the game move 10x slower than Papers, Please or Orwell. And even though many games in this genre do have different routes for your decision, this game force you into choices. Characters will add themselves to your contacts even if you refuse (by giving you "an offer you cannot refuse") and threaten you with game over if relationship is not maintained. Some story choice is an illusion that either do nothing or resulting in game over.

Neat concept, reasonably well executed by what I understand is a fairly novice indy team.

Wish there were more character customization options.

review_text_raw:
I backed this game on Kickstarter 3 or 4 years ago and forgot about it till now. For 15 dollars (I paid 12), this game has been worth every penny. I really enjoyed the progression of security rankings and the data and power that came along with them. I also liked the ironic naming of the Department of Liberty. The little news headlines were interesting to read and paralleled our society in a way that made me think "Could this be us someday?" 

I don't know if your overall play style affects the endgame but I chose to play as a ruthless arm of the state just to see how far I could take my power. In the end, I chose to [spoiler] become the new director of the all powerful DoL and take down Charles Douglas. [/spoiler] However, in real life I found myself disgusted at the choices I "had" to make in the name of security and personal gain. Just knowing that I was violating privacy AND potentially ruining lives was quite the experience. The people I betrayed and killed felt real and conflicting. But alas, [strike] control [/strike] ... I mean security above all else, no?

The game can be played all through a mouse. A couple times my CODEX world-map background refused to pop up until I clicked it or tried to scroll. The biometric data was a little graphically glitchy. A few times I was confused at new task assignment types but I figured it out. Overall, a polished game with little complaints especially for how affordable it is. 

It felt rewarding to see Clearance Level 1, Rank = 1st. The soundtrack was [b] beautiful, [/b] truly well composed. The game made me feel conflict and emotion which is indicative of an excellent work of media/art/etc. If you are interested in surveillance, politics, culture, RPG's, or conflict this game is for you. After my play-through, I can't help to reflect on our own society and how much this game may or may not be representative of our current (and future) society. Excellent job Monomyth Games, kudos for this excellent game!

review_text_raw:
This game is not without it's problems, but for it's price, and the assumption that the problems will be fixed, I personally think it's worth a playthrough, especially if commentary on Orwellian government is something that interests you. Having finished the game once, I'm unsure if there are points of divergence in the story, but I do know there are conditions where
you fail and have to restart, and there are in fact multiple endings.

Pros:
-Engaging storyline.
-Pretty interface, actually makes you feel like you're sitting in an office doing this stuff.
-Simple, easy to follow gameplay, most of the time.
-Lots of different actions you can take make it feel like you're doing different things even though you aren't really.
-The mission where you interrogate the guy was REALLY fun and I wish they had more of those.

Cons:
-Gameplay can be frustrating at times, particularly on a certain mission type where it's unclear which power you are meant to use to Discard/Ignore/NoMatch people, and using the wrong power makes you lose compliance.
-Minor spelling errors littered throughout the game.
-Certain parts ("post-mission missions") can be really boring, but they are fast and even skippable.
-Certain bugs, but nothing gamebreaking. For instance, there was one case of 3 pieces of evidence having to be linked, but you can only link 2 at once.
-Clarity on which tool to use could be better, but that's more my fault on not paying attention.
-Interface clunky at times.

Overall, I'd say 6.5/10. This game, like I said, is not without it's flaws, but they can be corrected, and if you like the concept and you liked Papers Please, you'll have a fun time with this. The pros do outweigh the cons, though it can be a bit of a slog to get through sometimes and it can be a bit frustrating. At the end of the day, for 15 bucks, it's worth a playthrough.

Having waited a long time since the Kickstarter ended I was really excited for this game. Then in the first playthrough I failed the Tutorial... which was surprising, I didn't think that was possible to do that. My first game was a mess, particularly due to the scaling of UI and the controls were not very clear. I failed the timed mission and wasn't really getting into the story at all because of frustration. 

Maybe a day or two later update 1.14 came through and it changed everything for the better. I can see everything in the foreground/background, stop the map from spinning the targets out of view and actually focus on the tasks.

These choices were a big part of the pull of this game for me. Do I sell Torrent users data to the DoL Agent to buy the Camera Drone, or sell instead to the underground hackers aiming to expose the DoL system? Should I help my sister with her money trouble before she will admit about it to me, what if I don't?

The game is good, better after the first hour definitely. Many people mention Papers, Please and I can see that too. Once you get past CL10 and the missions start to open up a bit it is a much better experience, I'm looking forward to breaking into CL7 very soon.

Also, for now, Monomyth are updating things pretty regularly and making noticable differences to the performance and interface for Need To Know. Its worth a try!
